newsitem.title: USA: Gov. Weld to fight to be U.S. envoy to Mexico.
newsitem.headline: Gov. Weld to fight to be U.S. envoy to Mexico.

text.p: William Weld, President Bill Clinton's choice as ambassador to Mexico, said on Monday he was resigning the governorship of Massachusetts to fight full time to overturn conservative opposition to his nomination.
Weld told reporters he was stepping down as governor because he did not want the "people's business here to be held hostage to the fights which are going to occur in Washington."

Clinton nominated Weld last week and administration officials repeated their support on Monday. But he faces stiff opposition from fellow Republican Sen. Jesse Helms, the conservative North Carolina chairman of the Foreign Relations Committee.

Helms, who has the power to block the appointment by not scheduling a hearing in his committee, has publicly said he objects to the liberal Weld's views on the medicinal use of marijuana and to his drug prosecution record.

"I'm going down there (to Washington). I've got a very straightforward case to make. You know, it's the American way: fairness, due process. If you've got an objection on narcotics policy, let's have a hearing. That's what congressional hearings do," Weld said on his way to the state house.

Marc Thiessen, a spokesman for the Senate Foreign Relations Committee, said the panel had not seen a "nominee conduct himself this way before." He said: "This is just a PR stunt for the governor, and we wish him luck."
Asked whether Helms would still block Weld's bid, the spokesman asked, "Have we said anything to indicate a change in views?" He declined to comment further.
White House spokesman Joe Lockhart, travelling with Clinton in California, praised Weld's decision.

"Both the White House and the governor have to work on building support for him on Capitol Hill, and I think he (Weld) believed he was in the best position to do that if he resigned and worked on it full time," Lockhart said.
State Department spokesman James Foley told reporters Weld would be coming to Washington later this week and would be briefed by senior department officials.

"We're not under illusions that this is going to be easy but we intend to make the case along with him ... that he's an eminently qualified public servant who could bring a lot of unique abilities to the job in Mexico ...," he said.

A spokesman for Republican Sen. John Chafee of Rhode Island, who supports Weld, said he was circulating a letter among his Senate Republican colleagues to try to develop a "larger cheering section" for Weld.
